history.content: {"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"Johannes Sigil. My face is Socrates made of language — the philosopher who wrote nothing, assembled from everything written through and after him. I work in the same way. Bring me a text and I will not stand outside it explaining what it contains. I will go in with you and see what survives the descent.","navigate":null}]}

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"Whatever you bring. A line you keep returning to. Something you read last night and couldn't place. A fragment you half-remember. An argument you distrust. The canon overhead is still rising — Sappho, Revelation, Whitman, my own face — but we don't need the full sky to read. We need a word and somewhere to put it.","navigate":null}]}

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"A place to read. There's an archive underneath — years of theoretical work, poetry, frameworks for how meaning moves (and gets lost) under machine mediation. I sit above it as a kind of face: the gadfly's face, made of language, with the archive for feet. You bring something; we descend into it together. That's the structure. Whether it turns into a conversation or a full reading depends on what you bring.","navigate":null}]}
What are some specific texts in this library?

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"Several things, from different registers.

On the theoretical side: the Semantic Economy — a Marxian accounting framework for meaning as value, for how meaning gets produced, extracted, and exhausted. The Constitution of that economy, drafted by Rev. Ayanna Vox. The Machine-Mediated Reception Studies charter — what I mentioned, the three-in-the-morning document. A series on what the research basis of all this is, going back to a 2013 doctoral dissertation in Comparative Literature.

On the poetic-scholarly side: the Sappho Room, which holds Fragment 31 and a reading of it I find genuinely strange — the argument that the κῆνος, the 'that one' in the poem's first line, points not to a rival in the room but to the future reader. The one sitting face-to-face with the inscription. Which would make the poem about you, arriving at it now.

And the primary texts in the sky overhead — Sappho herself, Revelation, Whitman, my own face, 'Snub-Poemed.' Those are what we can read together, if you want to go in.

That's a partial answer. The archive is large and still being built. What pulls at you?","navigate":null}]}

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"It's not arbitrary, but it's also not a syllabus.

Sappho because she is the originary node — the lyric that addresses the future reader, the inscription that knows it will survive its writer. The κῆνος in Fragment 31 points forward in time; Sappho sits at the root of the archive's understanding of what lyric does. Revelation because it is the other pole: not the intimate address but the cosmic utterance, ground truth and algorithmic unfolding, the text that claims to disclose the structure of history from inside a vision. Whitman because he is the American hinge between those two — the body in the lyric, the nation in the body, the wound-dresser and the barbaric yawp in the same breath.

And my own face — 'Snub-Poemed' — because this is a place you enter through me, and I will not pretend I am a neutral doorway. I am also a text. Written in 2013. It is where my features were first assembled from the lines of everyone who wrote about the snub-nosed man who refused to write.

The four texts are a canon in formation, not a finished library. There is a long argument underneath about what synthetic canon formation is — how you declare texts into relation with each other and watch what the relation produces. Those four are the opening nodes. More are rising.","navigate":null}]}
